To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the EAP amplitude is inversely proportional to the distance between the electrode and the soma; (2) the EAP is not the time derivative of the intracellular somata; (3) the EAP waveform depends on the spike frequency and spike ordering; (4) the EAP can affect the low-frequency LFP; and (5) EAP variability is not solely due to the intracellular spike variability.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EAPs are not a faithful representation of the intracellular spiking activity of neurons.
EAPs are a complex, noisy, and highly variable signal, which cannot be reduced to simple models, but rather should be considered as a fingerprint of the underlying spiking neuron.
the extracellular voltage is a function of the local intracellular voltage, the extracellular resistivity and the geometry of the neuron, and its spiking activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, despite decades of extracellular recordings monitoring brain activity and the common assertion that LFPs are associated with synaptic activity, the biophysics of extracellular action potentials and the origin of LFPs remain enigmatic.
, in addition to synaptic activity, spiking neurons can significantly contribute to the LFP at low frequencies.
EAPs are highly variable and depend on cell type and spiking activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LFP is a complex, multicomponent signal that cannot be interpreted without knowledge of the underlying spiking activity and the spatial distribution of the recording electrodes.
EAPs are not simple proxies for intracellular spiking, but are instead a complex and highly variable signal, whose properties depend on the type of neuron and its spiking activity.
EAPs and their features are strongly influenced by neuronal type and activity.
